# Vignette: Youssef

Youssef is a 55-year-old married farmer who came to this country from Syria twelve years ago and has spent the better part of a decade building a small but productive life on a few acres of leased land outside the city. He grows vegetables — tomatoes, cucumbers, herbs — and sells them at local markets on weekends. His wife, Fatima, helps him with the harvest. Until about eight months ago, he describes his life as quiet and purposeful, the kind of life he had worked hard to construct after leaving everything behind in Syria.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Youssef had stayed later than usual at his roadside stand, waiting for a final customer who never came. As he was loading unsold produce into his truck in the near-dark, two men approached him. What followed lasted perhaps four minutes. They beat him with their fists and with something hard — he believes a pipe, though he never saw it clearly — took his cash box and his phone, and left him on the ground beside his truck. A passing driver found him and called for help. He sustained a fractured orbital bone, three broken ribs, and lacerations to his face and scalp. He spent two nights in the hospital. His wife was called. He remembers feeling, above all, profoundly ashamed that she had to see him like that.

He returned to the farm within two weeks because, as he puts it, the plants do not wait. But something had shifted in a way he could not explain to Fatima or to himself. He began waking at two or three in the morning, heart hammering, certain that someone was outside the house. He would lie rigid in the dark, listening, sometimes for an hour or more before exhaustion took him back under. The dreams, when they came, were not always exact replays of the assault — sometimes they were older, darker scenes from Syria, as though the beating had broken open something he had kept sealed for years. He does not speak of Syria easily, but he acknowledges that the two things have become tangled together inside him in a way that frightens him.

During the day, he finds himself unable to work the far end of his fields, the section that borders a narrow road and sits out of sight of the farmhouse. He parks his tractor at the edge and turns back. He tells himself there is always something else to do closer in. He knows this is not true. When cars slow near his stand now, his body responds before his mind does — his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and he has to grip the table edge to keep himself from simply walking away. He has stopped staying past four in the afternoon. He has stopped going out after dark entirely.

Fatima has noticed. She asks him questions he deflects with short answers. He does not want her to worry, and he does not want to appear weak in front of a woman who has already watched him lose so much. He eats less than he used to. He has lost weight his frame cannot spare. He describes a persistent sense that the world has become unreliable in a fundamental way — that safety was always an illusion he had simply been lucky enough to maintain for a while.

What troubles him most, he says, is the anger. He has always been a patient man. He was patient with the land, with difficult customers, with bureaucracy, with loss. But now he finds himself flaring at small things — a stuck gate latch, a late delivery, a neighbor's dog. Afterward he feels disgusted with himself. He does not recognize the person he is becoming. He came to the market one Saturday, looked out at the crowd of strangers moving toward him, and simply could not make himself get out of the car. He drove home and told Fatima the engine was making a noise. He sat in the driveway for a long time before going inside.
